title: 11 Effects of limit fed diets with varying levels of a roughage pellet on performance of growing beef cattle
content:
Abstract
One hundred twenty crossbred beef steers were used in two periods (n =60 head per block; average BW = 266 ± 23 kg) to evaluate the effects of three levels of roughage pellet (RP) inclusion 10%, 15% or 20% of the diet (as fed basis) compared to a diet containing 10% cottonseed hull (CH; as-fed basis) in limit fed growing diets for beef cattle. Prior to the initiation of the study steers had been grazing annual ryegrass. At the initiation of the study, steers were removed off grass, shrunk overnight, weighed then blocked by BW and assigned to pens, and pens were randomly assigned to treatments. Diets were fed twice daily to target 2.25% of body weight (BW) on a dry matter (DM) basis. Cattle were weighed on d 28, 56 and 84. Feed delivery was adjusted to reflect the new pen weight on those days. Pen was the experimental unit, treatment was the fixed effect, block and period were considered random effects. Performance data were analyzed using PROC MIXED of SAS, and health data (non-parametric) were analyzed using PROC GLIMMIX of SAS. On days 28, 56, and 84, steers fed the 10% RP diet had greater BW compared to those fed CH and steers fed the 20% RP diet (P ≤ 0.05). Average daily gain (ADG) was also greatest for the 10% RP group during both the initial period (days 0-28) and the overall study duration (days 0-84; P ≤ 0.005). No differences in ADG were observed during the intermediate period (days 0-56; P = 0.48). Dry matter intake (DMI) did not differ among treatments at any point during the study. Gain-to-feed ratio (G:F) was greatest for the 10% RP group compared to the CH group during both the initial period (days 0-28) and the overall study duration (days 0-84; P < 0.02). Health observations included one case of bloat in the CH treatment and four cases in the 20% RP treatment (P ≥ 0.76). Results indicate that RP can be a suitable replacement for traditional roughage sources in limit fed diets without negatively affecting performance.
